claim: One of the most common distinctions in long-term memory is that between semantic (i.e., general world knowledge) and episodic (i.e., recollection of contextually specific events from one's past).
source: One of the most common distinctions in long-term memory is that between semantic (i.e., general world knowledge) and episodic (i.e., recollection of contextually specific events from one's past).
evidence: This is a foundational claim in memory research supported by established scientific consensus and citations in the introduction.

claim: Emerging cognitive neuroscience data suggest a surprisingly large overlap between the neural correlates of semantic and episodic memory.
source: However, emerging cognitive neuroscience data suggest a surprisingly large overlap between the neural correlates of semantic and episodic memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research findings discussed in the introduction.

claim: Personal semantic memories (i.e., knowledge about the self and one's life) have been studied little and do not easily fit into the standard semantic-episodic dichotomy.
source: Moreover, personal semantic memories (i.e., knowledge about the self and one's life) have been studied little and do not easily fit into the standard semantic-episodic dichotomy.
evidence: This claim is supported by the literature review and citations discussing personal semantics.

claim: All four types of memory (general facts, autobiographical facts, repeated events, and unique events) involved activity within a common network bilaterally including frontal pole, paracingulate gyrus, medial frontal cortex, middle/superior temporal gyrus, precuneus, posterior cingulate, angular gyrus, and some areas of the medial temporal lobe.
source: In multivariate analysis, all four types of memory involved activity within a common network bilaterally (e.g., frontal pole, paracingulate gyrus, medial frontal cortex, middle/superior temporal gyrus, precuneus, posterior cingulate, angular gyrus) and some areas of the medial temporal lobe.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the fMRI data analysis results presented in the study.

claim: The four memory types differentially engaged the common network, increasing in activity from general to autobiographical facts, from autobiographical facts to repeated events, and from repeated to unique events.
source: Yet the four memory types differentially engaged this network, increasing in activity from general to autobiographical facts, from autobiographical facts to repeated events, and from repeated to unique events.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fMRI data showing graded patterns of activation across memory types.

claim: The data are compatible with a component process model, in which declarative memory types rely on different weightings of the same elementary processes, such as perceptual imagery, spatial features, and self-reflection.
source: Our data are compatible with a component process model, in which declarative memory types rely on different weightings of the same elementary processes, such as perceptual imagery, spatial features, and self-reflection.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the pattern of results observed in the study.

claim: The semantic-episodic distinction is classic and remains crucial for cognition and neuroscience today.
source: This distinction is classic (Herrmann, 1982; Renoult and Rugg, 2020) and remains crucial for cognition and neuroscience today.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical and contemporary literature.

claim: Semantic and episodic memory have been recognized as 'partially overlapping' since Tulving's 1972 work.
source: Importantly, although these two putative memory systems have long been recognized as 'partially overlapping' (Tulving, 1972) and interacting (Greenberg and Verfaellie, 2010), they have largely been investigated via separate research traditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tulving's foundational work.

claim: When comparing the general semantic network to the episodic core recollection network, it becomes evident that the two networks share midline frontal, middle temporal, parahippocampal, ventral parietal, and midline posterior regions.
source: For example, when one compares the functional neuroimaging findings from the semantic memory literature (a 'general semantic network'; Binder, 2016; Binder et al., 2009; Binder and Desai, 2011) to those from the episodic memory literature (an 'episodic core recollection network'; Rugg and Vilberg, 2013; Svoboda et al., 2006), it becomes evident that the two networks share the midline frontal, middle temporal, parahippocampal, ventral parietal, and midline posterior regions (Renoult et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple neuroimaging studies comparing semantic and episodic networks.

claim: The hippocampus can facilitate the acquisition and retrieval of a rich semantic network.
source: The hippocampus can facilitate the acquisition and retrieval of a rich semantic network (Blumenthal et al., 2017; Cutler et al., 2019; Klooster et al., 2020; Sheldon and Moscovitch, 2012), partly through relational processing (Duff et al., 2019) or pattern completion (Solomon and Schapiro, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent research on hippocampal function.

claim: Anterior hippocampal atrophy features in neurodegenerative diseases affecting semantic and episodic memory alike.
source: Anterior hippocampal atrophy features in neurodegenerative diseases affecting semantic and episodic memory alike (Chapleau et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical research on neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: The lateral anterior temporal lobe may be involved in episodic recollection, as shown by its recruitment when successfully learning word pairs.
source: Similarly, the lateral anterior temporal lobe may also be involved in episodic recollection, as shown by its recruitment when successfully learning word pairs (de Chastelaine et al., 2016; Renoult et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing anterior temporal lobe involvement in episodic tasks.

claim: Personal semantics includes personal factual knowledge, such as autobiographical facts, and knowledge of repeated personally experienced events.
source: Personal semantics includes personal factual knowledge, such as autobiographical facts (e.g., I am adept at yoga), and knowledge of repeated personally experienced events, including contextual details that have been abstracted across several instances (e.g., my yoga routine when going to the gym).
evidence: This is a definitional claim based on the taxonomy of personal semantics discussed in the literature.

claim: Memories of unique and repeated episodes are often impaired together in amnesic patients, whereas knowledge of general and personal facts are typically better preserved.
source: For instance, in amnesic patients, memories of unique and repeated episodes are often impaired together, whereas knowledge of general and personal facts are typically better preserved (reviewed in Renoult et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a review of clinical studies on amnesic patients.

claim: Personal semantics has been reported to be the most common form of autobiographical memory elicited in free and cued recall.
source: Personal semantics is an understudied form of memory relative to semantic and episodic memory, even though it has been reported to be the most common form of autobiographical memory elicited in free and cued recall (Barsalou, 1988), and in brain stimulation studies (Curot et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies on autobiographical memory retrieval.

claim: Repeated events induce a greater facilitation of specific event retrieval than autobiographical facts.
source: Personal semantics play an important role in the retrieval of specific events (Conway, 1987; Conway and Pleydell-Pearce, 2000; Haque and Conway, 2001), and such facilitation can vary with the type of personal semantics (e.g., repeated events induce a greater facilitation than autobiographical facts; Sheldon et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study comparing types of personal semantics.

claim: Autobiographical facts have been associated with greater activity in the left medial frontal cortex and retrosplenial cortex than general facts.
source: Autobiographical facts have been associated with greater activity in the left medial frontal cortex and retrosplenial cortex than general facts (Maguire and Frith, 2003), but have not differed in lateral temporal activity (Maguire and Frith, 2003; Maguire and Mummery, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific neuroimaging studies comparing autobiographical and general facts.

claim: Repeated events have elicited less activity than unique events in the frontal pole, parahippocampal gyrus, posterior cingulate, and precuneus.
source: Repeated events have elicited less activity than unique events in the frontal pole, parahippocampal gyrus, posterior cingulate, and precuneus (Ford et al., 2011; Holland et al., 2011; Levine et al., 2004), but not differed in hippocampal activity (notably, Addis et al., 2004a; Addis et al., 2004b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple neuroimaging studies comparing repeated and unique events.

claim: Several neuroimaging studies have reported a graded increase in activity across semantic memories, autobiographical facts, and episodic memories in medial prefrontal, temporal polar, and retrosplenial cortex.
source: For instance, several neuroimaging studies have reported a graded increase in activity across semantic memories, autobiographical facts, and episodic memories in medial prefrontal, temporal polar, and retrosplenial cortex (Maguire, 2001; Maguire and Frith, 2003; Maguire and Mummery, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies showing graded patterns of activation.

claim: In a recent event-related potential study, both types of personal semantics produced intermediate mean amplitudes for the N400 and for the late positive component, compared to general facts and unique events.
source: In a recent event-related potential study (Renoult et al., 2016) that compared semantic memory (i.e., general facts), two types of personal semantics (i.e., autobiographical facts and repeated events) and episodic memory (i.e., unique events), a similar graded pattern occurred. Both types of personal semantics produced intermediate mean amplitudes for the N400, an index of semantic processing (Kutas and Federmeier, 2011), and for the late positive component, an index of episodic processing (Rugg and Curran, 2007), compared to general facts and unique events (Renoult et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific ERP study by the authors.

claim: The two types of personal semantics (autobiographical facts and repeated events) did not differ from one another in the N400 and late positive component amplitudes.
source: The two types of personal semantics did not differ from one another in this study (Renoult et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific finding from the ERP study.

claim: The study used fMRI to record brain activity while 48 participants verified statements concerning general facts, autobiographical facts, repeated events, and unique events.
source: Here, we used fMRI to record brain activity while 48 participants verified statements concerning general facts, autobiographical facts, repeated events, and unique events.
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the study design.

claim: The comparison of semantic and episodic memory types in this study is unbiased by response time differences between conditions.
source: Further, even though semantic and episodic retrieval typically involve different retrieval times, our comparison of these memory types is unbiased by response time differences between conditions (Renoult et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the study design, supported by reference to a previous study.

claim: Self-relevance was lowest for general facts compared to all personal forms of memory in the behavioral study.
source: Self-relevance was lowest for general facts compared to all personal forms of memory, and lower for personal semantics (i.e., autobiographical facts and repeated events) than unique events (see Table 1 and Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1A.

claim: Self-relevance was lower for personal semantics (autobiographical facts and repeated events) than unique events.
source: Self-relevance was lowest for general facts compared to all personal forms of memory, and lower for personal semantics (i.e., autobiographical facts and repeated events) than unique events (see Table 1 and Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1A.

claim: The amount of visual detail increased from general facts to autobiographical facts to repeated events to unique events.
source: Additionally, the amount of visual detail increased from general facts to autobiographical facts to repeated events to unique events (see Table 1 and Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1B.

claim: A smaller proportion of general facts evoked a scene compared to the three personal memory types.
source: A smaller proportion of general facts evoked a scene compared to the three personal memory types (see Table 2 and Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Table 2 and Figure 2C.

claim: A smaller proportion of autobiographical facts elicited images of a scene compared to repeated events and unique events.
source: Similarly, a smaller proportion of autobiographical facts elicited images of a scene compared to repeated events and unique events.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data on scene imagery.

claim: Repeated events and unique events did not differ in the proportion of memories perceived as scenes.
source: Repeated events and unique events did not differ in the proportion of memories perceived as scenes (see Appendix 1 for the statistical tests of vague/nothing and object responses).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data on scene imagery.

claim: The linear contrast and facts vs. events contrast were both significant (ps < .001) in the non-rotated PLS analysis.
source: The linear contrast and facts vs. events contrast were significant (ps < .001), explaining 48.78% and 51.22% of the cross-block covariance respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical results of the PLS analysis.

claim: The linear contrast explained 48.78% of the cross-block covariance.
source: The linear contrast and facts vs. events contrast were significant (ps < .001), explaining 48.78% and 51.22% of the cross-block covariance respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical results of the PLS analysis.

claim: The facts vs. events contrast explained 51.22% of the cross-block covariance.
source: The linear contrast and facts vs. events contrast were significant (ps < .001), explaining 48.78% and 51.22% of the cross-block covariance respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical results of the PLS analysis.

claim: The conditions were maximally dissociated at the seventh lag (8.4 s post cue onset) during the response screen.
source: The temporal 'brain scores' show that the conditions were maximally dissociated at the seventh lag, that is the seventh brain volume after the first acquisition or 8.4 s post cue onset, during the response screen (see Figures 3c and 4c and Appendix 4—figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal analysis of brain scores shown in the figures.

claim: The linear contrast showed that activity increased from general to autobiographical facts, from autobiographical facts to repeated events, and from repeated to unique events bilaterally in large regions of the frontal cortex (frontal pole, paracingulate gyrus, frontal medial cortex), precuneus, posterior cingulate cortex, retrosplenial cortex, angular gyrus, and with activity of the right middle frontal gyrus, left parahippocampal gyrus, left hippocampus, and left middle and superior temporal gyrus.
source: The linear contrast showed that activity increased from general to autobiographical facts, from autobiographical facts to repeated events, and from repeated to unique events bilaterally in the large regions of the frontal cortex (frontal pole, paracingulate gyrus, frontal medial cortex), precuneus, posterior cingulate cortex, retrosplenial cortex, angular gyrus, and with activity of the right middle frontal gyrus, left parahippocampal gyrus, left hippocampus, and left middle and superior temporal gyrus (see Figures 3 and 5, Table 3, and Appendix 2 for additional lags).
evidence: This claim is supported by the fMRI results for the linear contrast shown in figures and tables.

claim: Activity progressively decreased from general to autobiographical facts, from autobiographical facts to repeated events, and from repeated to unique events in areas of the right frontal inferior gyrus, superior parietal lobule, supramarginal gyrus, and bilateral lateral occipital cortex.
source: Activity progressively decreased from general to autobiographical facts, from autobiographical facts to repeated events, and from repeated to unique events in areas of the right frontal inferior gyrus, superior parietal lobule, supramarginal gyrus, and bilateral lateral occipital cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fMRI results for the linear contrast.

claim: Activity in several regions of the 'core memory network' dissociated the four memory conditions from the control condition, including in the inferior/middle frontal gyrus, caudate, lingual gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, and hippocampus bilaterally, and the left middle/superior temporal gyrus.
source: Activity in several regions of the 'core memory network' (Addis et al., 2016; Burianova and Grady, 2007; Rugg and Vilberg, 2013; Svoboda et al., 2006) dissociated the four memory conditions from the control condition, including in the inferior/middle frontal gyrus, caudate, lingual gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, and hippocampus bilaterally, and the left middle/superior temporal gyrus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fMRI results comparing memory conditions to control, with citations to the core memory network literature.

claim: The facts vs. events contrast showed that regions including frontal pole, precuneus, posterior cingulate, angular gyrus, and middle frontal gyrus bilaterally, and left parahippocampal gyrus, left hippocampus, and left middle/superior temporal gyrus were associated with greater activity for events than facts.
source: The facts vs. events contrast was similar to the linear contrast (see Figures 4 and 5, Table 4, and Appendix 3 for additional lags) with the first set of regions (i.e., frontal pole, precuneus, etc.) being associated with greater activity for events than facts, and the second set of regions (i.e., right frontal inferior gyrus, etc.) being associated with reduced activity for events than facts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fMRI results for the facts vs. events contrast shown in figures and tables.

claim: General and autobiographical facts did not differ in how well they expressed the 'facts' portion of the latent variable in the facts vs. events contrast.
source: In supplementary analyses, the statistical comparison of brain scores showed that general and autobiographical facts did not differ in how well they expressed the 'facts' portion of the LV, and repeated and unique events did not differ in how well they expressed the 'events' portion of the LV (see Appendix 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by supplementary statistical analyses of brain scores.

claim: Repeated and unique events did not differ in how well they expressed the 'events' portion of the latent variable in the facts vs. events contrast.
source: In supplementary analyses, the statistical comparison of brain scores showed that general and autobiographical facts did not differ in how well they expressed the 'facts' portion of the LV, and repeated and unique events did not differ in how well they expressed the 'events' portion of the LV (see Appendix 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by supplementary statistical analyses of brain scores.

claim: The findings are compatible with a continuum perspective of declarative memory, because quantitative rather than qualitative variations in brain activity suffice to characterize the relation between these memory types.
source: These findings are compatible with a continuum perspective of declarative memory, because quantitative rather than qualitative variations in brain activity suffice to characterize the relation between these memory types (Renoult et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the pattern of results, supported by citation to the continuum perspective.

claim: Repeated events are generally remembered less vividly than unique events, with reduced temporal specificity, personal significance, emotionality, and amount of details.
source: For example, as compared to unique events, repeated events are generally remembered less vividly: they are associated with reduced temporal specificity, personal significance, emotionality, and amount of details (e.g., Addis et al., 2004b; Holland et al., 2011; Levine et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies comparing repeated and unique events.

claim: Both memories of unique and repeated events share a spatial organization that gives them their 'basic context', as well as a first person perspective and detailed visual imagery.
source: This is consistent with the idea that both memories of unique and repeated events share a spatial organization that gives them their 'basic context', as well as a first person perspective, detailed visual imagery (Hassabis and Maguire, 2007; Nadel, 1991; Robin, 2018; Robin et al., 2016; Rubin, 2022; Rubin and Umanath, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on scene construction and event memory.

claim: Scenes are thought to be a dominant and integral feature of events.
source: Thus, scenes are thought to be a dominant and integral feature of events (Hassabis and Maguire, 2007; Nadel, 1991; Robin, 2018; Robin et al., 2016; Rubin, 2022; Rubin and Umanath, 2015) in a way that has not been argued for 'facts'.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on scene construction and event memory.

claim: The core network (default mode network) has been subdivided into an anterior temporal network linked to 'entities' or 'conceptual remembering' and a posterior medial network linked to 'situational models' or 'perceptual remembering'.
source: The core network, also known as the default mode network, has been subdivided into an anterior temporal network linked to 'entities' (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Reagh and Ranganath, 2018) or 'conceptual remembering' (Sheldon et al., 2019) and a posterior medial network linked to 'situational models' (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Reagh and Ranganath, 2018) or 'perceptual remembering' (Sheldon et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on the functional subdivisions of the default mode network.

claim: Neither the anterior temporal network nor the posterior medial network is strictly dedicated to semantic or episodic memory.
source: Although these networks process different kinds of information, neither is strictly dedicated to semantic or episodic memory (Reagh and Ranganath, 2018; Sheldon et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research on network function.

claim: The dissociation between general/autobiographical facts and repeated/unique events did not have a clear posterior medial to anterior temporal demarcation in this study.
source: Accordingly, in our study the dissociation between general/autobiographical facts and repeated/unique events did not have a clear posterior medial to anterior temporal demarcation (i.e., posterior medial activity for events and anterior temporal activity for facts).
evidence: This claim is based on the fMRI results showing the pattern of activation across networks.

claim: Regions primarily within the posterior medial network (angular gyrus, posterior cingulate gyrus, precuneus, and parahippocampal gyrus) dissociated memory conditions, whereas those within the anterior temporal network did not.
source: Instead, regions primarily within the posterior medial network (i.e., angular gyrus, posterior cingulate gyrus, precuneus, and parahippocampal gyrus; Ritchey et al., 2015) dissociated memory conditions, whereas those within the anterior temporal network (i.e., frontal orbital cortex, inferior anterior temporal gyrus, temporal pole, bilateral amygdala, and perirhinal cortex; Ritchey et al., 2015) did not.
evidence: This claim is based on the fMRI results showing differential activation patterns across networks.

claim: Many regions of the posterior medial network were associated with greater activity for repeated/unique events than general/autobiographical facts.
source: Further, cues were more temporally specific for repeated/unique events than general/autobiographical facts. Consistent with this, many regions of the posterior medial network were associated with greater activity for repeated/unique events than general/autobiographical facts (similar to Ford et al., 2011; Levine et al., 2004; Maguire and Mummery, 1999), and showed a linear increase from the most general type of memory (i.e., general facts) to the most specific memory (i.e., unique events).
evidence: This claim is based on the fMRI results and is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: Activity in regions associated with visuospatial processing (e.g., precuneus) and scenes (e.g., medial temporal regions) coheres with behavioral data to support the prominence of contextual specificity in determining the relation across memory types.
source: Therefore, activity in regions associated with visuospatial processing (e.g., precuneus) and scenes (e.g., medial temporal regions) coheres with behavioral data to support the prominence of contextual specificity in determining the relation across memory types.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim integrating fMRI and behavioral results.

claim: Activity in medial frontal regions increases along a continuum of contextual specificity, in harmony with ratings of visual details and scene perception.
source: Activity in medial frontal regions is in harmony with ratings of visual details and scene perception, likewise increasing along a continuum of contextual specificity (see Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is based on the integration of fMRI and behavioral data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The anterior portion of the medial frontal cortex may correspond best to self-processing rather than 'situational' processing or mental time travel.
source: However, this anterior portion of the medial frontal cortex may correspond best to self-processing rather than 'situational' processing or mental time travel (Lieberman et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to research on medial frontal cortex function.

claim: A parsimonious explanation for the overlap in neural substrates of semantic and episodic memory is that they rely on similar elementary component processes.
source: A parsimonious explanation is that semantic and episodic memory rely on similar elementary component processes (Cabeza and Moscovitch, 2013; Larsen, 1992; Moscovitch, 1992; Rajah and McIntosh, 2005; Renoult et al., 2012; Rubin, 2022).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to component process models.

claim: All types of memories would depend on a similar network of brain regions but with different weighting of certain nodes in the network.
source: All types of memories would depend on a similar network of brain regions but with different weighting of certain nodes in the network.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the component process model and the study's findings.

claim: Episodic memory would typically rely to a greater degree than semantic memory on rich sensory-perceptual imagery, complex situational models or scenes, spatial and temporal features, and self-reflection.
source: For instance, episodic memory would typically rely to a greater degree than semantic memory on rich sensory-perceptual imagery, complex situational models or scenes, spatial and temporal features, and self-reflection.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about component processes distinguishing memory types.

claim: Instead of activating different networks of brain regions, semantic and episodic processes may activate a similar network but with different degrees of magnitude, or recruit these brain regions in a complementary manner.
source: Accordingly, instead of activating different networks of brain regions, semantic and episodic processes may activate a similar network but with different degrees of magnitude, or recruit these brain regions in a complementary manner (Sherman et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citation and the study's findings.

claim: The neuroimaging data and complementary behavioral data are compatible with the component process view and inconsistent with strictly separated memory systems.
source: Our neuroimaging data, and complementary behavioral data obtained outside the scanner, are compatible with this component process view and inconsistent with strictly separated memory systems.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim summarizing the implications of the study's findings.

claim: The study included 48 participants in the fMRI analysis after exclusions.
source: Fifty-three recruited participants (35 women, 18 men) were aged 24.89 years on average (SD = 4.51; range: 19–34) and attained a mean of 16.43 years of education (SD = 2.42). This sample size was the largest that was possible to achieve. The sample size is larger than similar studies (e.g., N ~12–28; Addis et al., 2011; Burianova and Grady, 2007; Ford et al., 2011; Holland et al., 2011). No formal power analysis was conducted. Participants responded to ads on university campuses and on social media. Candidates were retained if they were right-handed, native English speakers, free of any contraindication for MRI (e.g., ferromagnetic metal, back pain, claustrophobia), aged between 18 and 35 years, and had not experienced head injury, or neurological and psychiatric disorders. We excluded three participants because of an inadvertent phase encoding switch, one for an incidental finding, and one for ineligibility.
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the sample after exclusions (53 recruited - 5 excluded = 48).

claim: The behavioral study included 106 participants after exclusions.
source: The total sample included 181 participants (143 women, 34 men, 2 non-binary; 2 missing values); they were 18.79 years old on average (SD = 1.58; range: 17–34; 2 missing values) and had attained a mean of 12.67 years of education (SD = 1.02; 3 missing values). The possible small differences between proximal memory types (e.g., Addis et al., 2004b; Maguire and Mummery, 1999; Renoult et al., 2016) justified the large sample size. We recruited participants from a pool of students who received a credit toward their introductory or research methods course. The ad specified the eligibility criteria, which were the same as the fMRI study apart from those for MRI safety. We excluded participants who disclosed information that conflicted with the criteria (n for primary reason listed): 18–35 years of age (n = 1), right-handed (n = 2), normal or corrected-to-normal vision (n = 1), no neurological or psychiatric disorder (past/present) or no loss of consciousness lasting more than 10 min (n = 26), and native English speakers (n = 35). We also excluded 1 participant for being inattentive during testing (i.e., looking at a cellphone during the task), and 9 for implausible data (i.e., always responding 'yes') or incomplete data (e.g., entire task or questionnaire). After exclusions we had a total of 106 participants (87 women, 19 men) with a mean age of 18.74 (SD = 1.05, range 18–23) and 12.67 years of education on average (SD = 0.97).
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the behavioral sample after exclusions.

claim: The four experimental conditions consisted of the same 70 main clauses.
source: The four experimental conditions (general facts, autobiographical facts, repeated events, unique events) consisted of the same 70 main clauses (material available in Appendix 5).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about stimulus design.

claim: The conditions differed in tense, with past tense for unique events, present perfect for repeated events, and present for facts.
source: The conditions differed in two aspects: (1) The tense changed from past tense for unique events, to present perfect for repeated events, to present for facts (general and autobiographical). The type of awareness associated with semantic memory is indeed thought to be centered in the present, whereas episodic recollection is oriented toward the past (Tulving, 2001; Tulving, 2002).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about stimulus design, with theoretical justification from citations.

claim: Distinct cue words preceded each condition and gave different degrees of temporal specificity.
source: (2) We added distinct cue words that preceded each condition and gave different degrees of temporal specificity. We used 6–7 cues per condition.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about stimulus design.

claim: In the unique events condition, specific time cues (last night, last week-end, this morning, this week, today, yesterday) were used to promote access to specific instances of events.
source: In the unique events condition, we used specific time cues (last night, last week-end, this morning, this week, today, yesterday) to promote access to specific instances of events (e.g., 'Yesterday, I took a picture').
evidence: This is a methodological claim about stimulus design for unique events.

claim: In the repeated events condition, script-like cues (when alone, when at a clinic, when at work, when on the bus, when on vacation, when shopping, when with friends) were used, constrained to events that happened repeatedly within the last year.
source: In the repeated events condition, we used script-like cues (when alone, when at a clinic, when at work, when on the bus, when on vacation, when shopping, when with friends), and constrained their temporal scope by asking participants to verify sentences by thinking about events that happened repeatedly within the last year (e.g., 'When shopping, I have taken a picture').
evidence: This is a methodological claim about stimulus design for repeated events.

claim: In the autobiographical facts condition, general time cues (everyday, often, rarely, sometimes, usually, very often) were used for participants to report what is usual for them.
source: In the autobiographical facts condition, we used general time cues (everyday, often, rarely, sometimes, usually, very often) for participants to report what is usual for them ('Very often, I take pictures').
evidence: This is a methodological claim about stimulus design for autobiographical facts.

claim: For the general facts condition, the first person personal pronoun (I) and the 6 cues were replaced by six distinct third person perspectives (everyone, few people, many people, most people, no one, some people), and participants had to report what they thought was generally true for people in their country.
source: For the general facts condition, the first person personal pronoun (I) and the 6 cues were replaced by six distinct third person perspectives (everyone, few people, many people, most people, no one, some people), and participants had to report what they thought was generally true for people in their country ('Few people take pictures').
evidence: This is a methodological claim about stimulus design for general facts.

claim: The cue was presented for approximately 2 s, followed by the main clause for approximately 4 s, and participants responded during a response screen that lasted approximately 3.5 s.
source: The cue (e.g., last weekend) was presented for ~2 s, followed with the main clause (e.g., I went to the pharmacy) for ~4 s. Participants responded after each statement during a response screen that lasted ~3.5 s and which displayed the response options.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about trial timing.

claim: Participants completed an odd/even task during a jittered interval that lasted from 0 to 12 s (mean of 4.6 s).
source: Participants completed an odd/even task during a jittered interval that lasted from 0 to 12 s (mean of 4.6 s; adapted from Madore et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the control task timing.

claim: Each of the seven runs included the four memory conditions, each comprising 10 trials.
source: Each of the seven runs included the four memory conditions, each comprising of 10 trials. A run lasted 10.6 min.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the experimental design.

claim: The MRI data were preprocessed using FMRIPREP version 1.2.3.
source: Results included in this manuscript come from preprocessing performed using fMRIPprep 1.2.3 (Esteban et al., 2018; Esteban et al., 2019), which is based on Nipype 1.1.6-dev (Gorgolewski et al., 2011; Gorgolewski et al., 2018; RRID:SCR_002502).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about data preprocessing.

claim: Multivariate analysis (partial least squares) was used to compare brain activity across the four memory conditions.
source: We leveraged multivariate analysis methods (i.e., partial least squares [PLS]; Krishnan et al., 2011; McIntosh et al., 2004a; McIntosh and Lobaugh, 2004b) to compare brain activity across these four memory conditions within a single analysis in a sample of 48 participants.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the analytical approach.

claim: The analytical approach tested whether data in the spatial and temporal domain explained adequately two hypothesized relations between memory conditions: (1) a continuum of contextual specificity, and (2) a dissociation between knowledge of facts and recollection of events.
source: Our analytical approach tested whether data in the spatial and temporal domain explained adequately two hypothesized relations between memory conditions: (1) a continuum of contextual specificity, and (2) a dissociation between knowledge of facts and recollection of events.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the hypotheses tested.

claim: Brain regions involved in visuospatial processing and imagery, like the precuneus, and in self-reflection, like the medial prefrontal cortex, should be more tightly associated with memories of unique events, and minimally associated with general factual knowledge.
source: Accordingly, brain regions involved in visuospatial processing and imagery, like the precuneus, and in self-reflection, like the medial prefrontal cortex, should be more tightly associated with memories of unique events, and minimally associated with general factual knowledge (Renoult et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on theoretical expectations and prior research.

claim: Brain regions known to have a crucial role in spatial processing and in representing scenes, such as the hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and retrosplenial cortex, should show greater activity for memories of unique and repeated events than for autobiographical and general facts.
source: Similarly, brain regions known to have a crucial role in spatial processing and in representing scenes, such as the hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and retrosplenial cortex, should show greater activity for memories of unique and repeated events than for autobiographical and general facts.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on theoretical expectations about scene processing.

claim: The visual details and scene components may depend on hippocampal processes, like relational or constructive processes, to some extent, as the association with a diverse source of personal information becomes stronger from general facts to unique events.
source: The visual details and scene components may depend on hippocampal processes, like relational (Duff et al., 2019) or constructive processes (Hassabis and Maguire, 2007; Schacter and Addis, 2007), to some extent, as the association with a diverse source of personal information becomes stronger from general facts to unique events (Sheldon et al., 2020; Sui and Humphreys, 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about hippocampal function supported by citations.

claim: The relations across memory types are not rigid and could be altered depending on task or personal goal.
source: Critically, however, our additional focus on component processes in the behavioral study (i.e., amount of visual details, ability to evoke a scene, self-relevance) relies on the theoretical perspective that relations between memory types can be explained through the information accessed and cognitive processes engaged. Thus, it is implicit to our approach that the relations across memory types are not rigid and could be altered depending on task or personal goal (e.g., Grilli and Verfaellie, 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the flexibility of memory type relations, supported by citation.

claim: The sample size of 48 participants is larger than similar studies (N ~12–28).
source: This sample size was the largest that was possible to achieve. The sample size is larger than similar studies (e.g., N ~12–28; Addis et al., 2011; Burianova and Grady, 2007; Ford et al., 2011; Holland et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological claim comparing sample size to prior studies.

claim: No formal power analysis was conducted for the fMRI study.
source: No formal power analysis was conducted.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about study design.

evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

evidence: This is a methodological claim about the behavioral study design.

claim: The facts vs. events contrast dominates to explain the spatiotemporal relations across memory conditions, although the difference in covariance explained between the two LVs of the non-rotated PLS was slight.
source: The non-rotated PLS converges with the data-driven PLS (see Appendix 4) to suggest the facts vs. events contrast dominates to explain the spatiotemporal relations across memory conditions, although the difference in covariance explained between the two LVs of the non-rotated PLS was slight.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the PLS results.

claim: Both a priori contrasts (linear and facts vs. events) captured aspects of the spatiotemporal relations adequately.
source: In fact, both a priori contrasts captured aspects of the spatiotemporal relations adequately.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the PLS results.

claim: Several regions showed a relatively small increase in activity from general facts to autobiographical facts, a relatively large increase from autobiographical facts to repeated events, and a relatively small increase from repeated events to unique events.
source: That is, activity increased (or decreased) continuously across memory types, but the extent of the increase (or decrease) confers greater similarity between general and autobiographical facts, and between repeated and unique events. Thus, several regions showed a relatively small increase in activity from general facts to autobiographical facts, a relatively large increase from autobiographical facts to repeated events, and a relatively small increase from repeated events to unique events; these include the precuneus, posterior cingulate, angular gyrus and middle frontal gyrus bilaterally, and left parahippocampal gyrus, left hippocampus, and left middle/superior temporal gyrus (see Appendix 2—figure 1 and Appendix 3—figure 1).
evidence: This is a descriptive claim about the pattern of activation based on fMRI data.

claim: Comparable non-rotated PLS results were obtained while including only voxels within the default mode and medial temporal networks from Barnett et al., 2021.
source: We obtained comparable non-rotated PLS results while including only voxels within the default mode and medial temporal networks from Barnett et al., 2021: 49.56% crossblock covariance (p < .001) for the linear contrast, and 50.44% crossblock covariance (p < .001) for the facts vs. events contrast.
evidence: This is a supplementary analysis result confirming the main findings within specific networks.

claim: The different types of cues used in the experiment were used to trigger different 'retrieval modes' in participants.
source: The different types of cues used in our experiment were used to trigger different 'retrieval modes' in our participants, 'a necessary condition for retrieval' (Tulving, 1983) that is maintained as a tonic state during a retrieval task (Rugg and Wilding, 2000).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the experimental manipulation, supported by citations.

claim: The behavioral data revealed the sentence cues induced typical phenomenological experience associated with these memory types.
source: The behavioral data revealed the sentence cues induced typical phenomenological experience associated with these memory types.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the behavioral results.

claim: The importance of visuospatial processes in subjective ratings and corresponding brain regions was not commensurate with characteristics of the stimuli, which differed little across conditions and primarily increased in temporal specificity.
source: In this study, the importance of visuospatial processes (in subjective ratings and corresponding brain regions) was not commensurate with characteristics of the stimuli, which differed little across conditions and primarily increased in temporal specificity (e.g., general facts: 'Most people wear jeans.'; autobiographical facts: 'Sometimes I wear jeans.'; repeated events: 'When at work, I have worn jeans.'; unique events: 'Yesterday, I wore jeans.').
evidence: This is an interpretive claim comparing stimulus characteristics to observed results.

claim: Knowledge can facilitate the search and construction of events.
source: For instance, knowledge can facilitate the search and construction of events (Irish and Piguet, 2013) and semantic memory can integrate contextual information (e.g., Greenberg et al., 2009; Sheldon and Moscovitch, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on the interaction between semantic and episodic memory.

claim: Semantic memory can integrate contextual information.
source: For instance, knowledge can facilitate the search and construction of events (Irish and Piguet, 2013) and semantic memory can integrate contextual information (e.g., Greenberg et al., 2009; Sheldon and Moscovitch, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on semantic memory.

claim: The additional concordance of medial frontal cortex with a continuum of contextual specificity could be a corollary of the strong links between aspects of self-relevance and episodic simulation.
source: The additional concordance of medial frontal cortex with a continuum of contextual specificity could be a corollary of the strong links between aspects of self-relevance and episodic simulation (Grysman et al., 2013; King et al., 2022; Tulving, 2002; Verfaellie et al., 2019), in addition to this region's role in modulating recollection (McCormick et al., 2020), for example through engaging schema-related information (Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about medial frontal cortex function, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Characteristics that would influence differences in hippocampal activity and other regions of the core memory network include: the number of details, their association, their integration within a scene or within a situational model, their coarseness and precision, their type and modality, their stability, as well as their projection into a temporally distant time, the open-endedness of the representation, the demands on pattern separation to construct unique representations or identify distinguishing features, and the likelihood of eliciting a specific event.
source: Some of the characteristics that would influence differences in hippocampal activity and other regions of the core memory network include: the number of details (Thakral et al., 2020), their association (Duff et al., 2019; Solomon and Schapiro, 2020), their integration within a scene (Nadel, 1991; Robin, 2018; Robin et al., 2016; Rubin and Umanath, 2015) or within a situational model (Reagh and Ranganath, 2018; Summerfield et al., 2010), their coarseness and precision (Craik, 2020; Ekstrom and Yonelinas, 2020), their type and modality (e.g., perceptual, spatial, temporal, social; Binder and Desai, 2011; Grilli and Verfaellie, 2016; Sheldon et al., 2019), their stability (Auger and Maguire, 2018), as well as their projection into a temporally distant time (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010), the open-endedness of the representation (Sheldon and Moscovitch, 2012), the demands on pattern separation to construct unique representations or identify distinguishing features (Rolls and Kesner, 2006; Schapiro et al., 2017), and the likelihood of eliciting a specific event (Renoult et al., 2015; Westmacott et al., 2004; Westmacott and Moscovitch, 2003).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about component processes, extensively supported by citations.

claim: How each component is involved would depend on the task at hand.
source: How each component is involved would also depend on the task at hand (e.g., Gurguryan and Sheldon, 2019); each component could be more or less engaged regardless of the memory type (e.g., semantic details can be thought of in rich detail, in relation to the self, or in relation to a spatial context).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the flexibility of component processes, supported by citation.

claim: There would be a 'neural-psychological representation correspondence' that includes elements of consciousness and that transcends categories of memory.
source: Therefore, there would be a 'neural-psychological representation correspondence' (Moscovitch and Gilboa, 2022) that includes elements of consciousness (e.g., feeling of being transported in time; Tulving, 2002) and that transcends categories of memory.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations.

claim: A taxonomy of personal semantics offers an opportunity to explore what brings all forms of memory together and what can sometimes pull them apart.
source: The operationalization of different types of personal semantics and their inclusion in a model of declarative memory does not promote fragmentation. Rather, a taxonomy of personal semantics offers an opportunity to explore what brings all forms of memory together and what can sometimes pull them apart.
evidence: This is a concluding theoretical claim about the value of the personal semantics framework.
